newsitem.title: UK: European gas oil arbitrage window to Asia closes.
newsitem.headline: European gas oil arbitrage window to Asia closes.

text.p: Asian demand for European gas oil has finally waned after two months leaving an uncertain future for the European market that has been underpinned by the eastern buying, traders said on Thursday.

Since the beginning of March Asia has drawn a touch over two million tonnes of European gas oil, much of it Russian, but rising European prices over the last few days combined with easing Singapore prices have shut the arbitrage window.
The spread between Russian prompt cif NWE gas oil against Singapore gas oil stands at a touch over $19 a tonne compared with $35 a tonne a week ago.

Freight rates have been high, up to $30 a tonne last week, but levels have eased as enquiries for tonnage declined. On Tuesday a 60,000 tonne tanker was fixed by an oil major to lift gas oil from the Med to Singapore at $22.50 a tonne.

The main driving force behind the strong prices in Singapore, Hin Leong Trading, is thought to have pulled out from its intense buying spree, which regularly set daily records for the amount of gas oil purchased.
Traders have commented that although Hin Leong may have outlets for the barrels acquired, those in the market that followed its lead may be left holding surplus barrels.
From the European angle Russian supplies of gas oil slowed noticeably in April, in part to meet increased domestic agricultural demand for harvest fuel.
Seaborne exports of Russian gas oil fell by 32 percent in April compared with March to 1.33 million tonnes from 1.96 million, according to figures released on Thursday by shipping inspectors Petrak.

The impact on European gas oil prices now the arb window has closed is not immediately clear since many in the market were anticipating just such a scenario developing. Several trading houses were avoiding arbing eastwards 10 days ago when the window was still open.

So far North European prices look firm both on futures and premiums. In the Mediterranean traders said physical length was becoming evident which had started to shave premiums. Swaps, however were noticeably weaker losing $2 a tonne on Thursday, trading at $8 under the screen from $6 under in the Med.
